Pour this mixture on top of the pumpkin, and then bake it off in a 375° oven for around an hour, or until the pumpkin is very soft.  It should start to look like pie crust; if it hasn't started to look like pie crust, add a little bit of water to the pan before the final bake. Finally, don’t worry too much about it actually being completely pumpkin pie.  There will be chunks of pumpkin mixed in, along with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and all the other spices, and also a bit of salt and sugar.  To assemble the pumpkin pie, top it all off with whipped cream (it even goes well with ice cream, if you care to serve it warm!), sprinkle with more powdered sugar, and enjoy!

prompt: Human: What can you tell me about the philosophy of John Locke
response:
Of all the philosophers who have influenced Western thought, John Locke may be the most influential for those who are thinking about pursuing a career in politics or law.  In particular, his views on government have been particularly influential in both political science and American law and politics.   If you’re just interested in philosophy as a whole, here are some of the core ideas about Locke you should try to understand:

Locke was a strong believer in the legitimacy of governments based almost entirely on their ability to protect citizens from harm.  While he did not actually believe this was possible, he believed people would come to believe it for themselves if governments did what they should do to keep them safe. 

Locke had a particular distrust of religious concepts that might allow bad rulers to manipulate people by convincing them the “God” they believed in was keeping an eye on them.  As the political theorist John Rawls has noted, Locke believed people would believe whatever rulers told them they were doing for their own good, whether it was really true or whether it could be proven false. 

Locke believed there should be no restrictions on people’s freedom of speech, thought or religion.  To him, all this should be able to lead to a more efficient, happier society and help people to enjoy their lives more.

Locke believed that people should have the opportunity to own property and make their own money.  But people should not own more than they could reasonably afford to keep themselves and their families alive. 

His view of what constitutes a “right” was very different than modern day American and Western philosophy.   In particular, he believed rights came not from the consent of the people, but rather from something within humans that makes them good citizens of a nation.   There is no concept of “constitutional” rights in Locke’s philosophy (as there is in the U.S.) and he did not think of the government as having the power to make any rules they wanted.

Locke was interested in the idea of “taboos”.  For example, in a free society we should not be shocked by seeing a parent abusing their child, or cheating on a spouse, or smoking, drinking and/or using drugs or committing suicide.   This sort of thing is considered acceptable practice in societies that value freedom.   In contrast, in a totalitarian society you can expect to face punishment unless you break some laws, and might even see the death penalty as acceptable if a government believed they deserved it.   Locke saw this sort of situation as one of its biggest problems and tried to fight against it in his philosophy by insisting on rights that people could not just break by simply refusing to obey rules about them.  

He also believed that there should be a separation of the church and state, but he didn’t want to put a wall between people and their God.   If there were no laws that said people had to believe in the God that the rulers used to be appointed by, they might still do what they believed was right in their hearts, and that could be very problematic for rulers and society as a whole.   But Locke’s belief in “taboos” also meant there was no real harm in using religion to justify what people did (for example, if a ruler said a death sentence in some cases was justified because the death penalty made the defendant’s life better).  This didn’t mean Locke believed this was right, but he did believe it was OK.  

Locke had a strong dislike of people not having the chance to defend themselves against others that might do them harm.  This included not having the knowledge to protect yourself in case of an accident, or not having an understanding of how to keep safe from physical harm or sexual assault.  

Locke was not very concerned with issues of women or minorities.   He had no particular problem with women’s emancipation and wanted to see that they should not be expected to be subservient to men, but rather that they should have equal rights to men.   He also believed people shouldn’t have to work to pay taxes if they wanted to avoid it and felt the concept of work itself was important to civilization.  If people were truly happy, they didn’t need to go to work, and some of the poorest people in history were not very unhappy.

As far as science goes, Locke believed that ideas should be accepted or rejected by the community as a whole, not just by experts or those people who had the same ideas as an expert.  This was a problem in that there were scientific communities that would do things for scientific reasons that weren’t in the common interest of society as a whole.  One example of this was when germ theory was developed, people would work very hard to show how harmful the bacteria were, even when it might hurt their professional reputation.   In contrast, Locke believed that ideas should be judged by their worth as a whole to the society it was being made for, based on whether it had the potential to help people, even if it hurt scientists personally.

prompt: Human: When were smart phones first made?
response:
Smart phones, as we currently know them, were first developed in the late 1990s by a group of engineers at Bell Labs in the United States. They were initially called “大哥大”, named after their size, but eventually their nickname stuck. 

In November 1993, AT&T and Lucent decided to compete with the Japanese mobile operators by developing a new type of cell phone. The idea was to put two small antennas on each piece of equipment and use a shared network to send text messages and fax messages.

As with many innovations from the 1990s, the first mobile phones ran on an OS called CP/M (Computing Systems Man-made, Inc.), which was later adopted as the first version of Windows by Microsoft. Bell Labs’ first prototype smartphone ran Linux, but it wasn’t until the second generation device that Windows found its way into it.

The idea was simple: the user would operate a phone by pushing buttons on the device. They would then communicate through a shared Wi-Fi network called CDMA, which is the type of technology used on most smart phones in the world today. Bell Labs’ prototype also used Bluetooth technology to transmit data between phones.

Bell Labs’ prototype was developed with software written by Peter Thimmesh, a researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Their work, which formed the basis of AT&T’s initial concept for a cell phone, was published in the August 1994 version of IEEE Communications Magazine.

AT&T received support from a number of companies for their mobile phone project and was able to obtain funding from Intel and the Department of Defense. In March 1995, AT&T partnered with Lucent to form the U.S. Cellnet Corporation. The two were able to secure the intellectual property associated with their work and the pair filed for patents in connection with the U.S. Cellnet’s development in September 1995 and October 1996.

AT&T became a competitor in the market when the first generation of smartphones were released in November 1996, with a major push by the company starting in the fourth quarter of 1997.

The first smartphones to hit the market were LG CD-200 and Samsung C100. IBM also released their IBM MobileFirst platform and BlackBerry released their BlackBerry Sync software and Bluetooth technology. 

By the summer of 1998, AT&T and Lucent signed contracts to manufacture mobile phones in two states: New York and Illinois, for a total of up to 15 manufacturing sites in each state. The first phone that was intended for commercial production was the C100, but many others were also on the way.

The C100 was initially released in the US in December 1996, followed by the C200 in April 1997. AT&T sold their original 5 million devices in the first half of 1998. They are credited with launching the personal mobile phone as we know it today. prompt: Human: I have to help plan a wedding and I have no experience with it. What are some things I need to know about wedding planning?
response:
Here’s what I know.  First off, a wedding is a big deal, and there’s a lot for you to do.  It’s a culmination of a long series of events, from the engagement to the bachelor and bachelorette parties.  You’ll often be assigned to work on one of these components, and you may find other people you work with to be equally involved, especially if you’re involved with logistics.  Wedding planning can be divided into many small components, which give it a much larger picture perspective.  This means a little planning can go a long way in saving time and stress later.  A great place to start is with your venue.  Most weddings will be held in a location that can be rented out by groups of people, such as a banquet hall, hotel or even an event space in a private residence, such as a barn or a cottage.  Other venues that are often selected for weddings include restaurants, performance venues, wedding chapels and parks.

Another aspect of wedding planning to consider is your budget.  Wedding planning is a big business, with vendors and planners charging according to a sliding scale, so be sure to find a person or company that works within your means.  It is important to also be careful about overspending, as your budget will largely depend on your personal financial status.

One more thing to think about is how many people you want to be involved, for obvious logistical reasons.  A wedding event will typically have at least the officiant, the bride/groom, their parents/cohabitants, any wedding party members, the photographer/video crew and themselves.  

What comes next is really the work involved in throwing the wedding.  This typically involves hiring the ceremony planner or officiant, the caterer, the bartender, the bartender, the wedding dress and tuxedo shop, the florist, the band and/or DJ, and the wedding planner.  If the couple likes to handle these details themselves, these should be candidates for being included in the budget as well.  
Once these services and supplies are hired, the couple should set out to research and select vendors and/or locations for all other supplies and services: the cake baker, the hair and makeup salon, the limo service, etc.  Most vendors will have a list of recommended services that they can recommend, which would be a good starting point when selecting a vendor.  
To ensure that each aspect is handled professionally, it can be helpful to create a checklist and timeline, and try to work as closely as possible with each vendor you choose.  

When all these details are finalized, the couple, the wedding party, the officiant and any other guests can be organized into their respective seating arrangements, and the couple can start choosing their wedding attire.  
Next up will be deciding where to get the rings, and planning on the way the wedding cake will be served.  Then the rehearsal will happen, and the bride and groom will probably try on their wedding outfits, giving feedback to the person helping with the final arrangements, whether it’s the wedding planner or a trusted friend.  The ceremony will take place, the first dance is usually chosen by the couple, and then the reception starts.  

I hope that this information is helpful as you start the job of planning a wedding!

(BTW, this site originally had a “How to Plan a Wedding” page, but it doesn’t exist anymore.  If you or someone you know needs help planning a wedding, please ask, we’d be happy to help!)

It sounds like the most straightforward recipe is the one without the canned pumpkin, but here are a couple other options:

Option 1: Make your own pie filling.  If you have access to canned pumpkin, you can make the pie filling as follows: 

•	1 can pumpkin (14 ounces), pureed
•	1 cup sugar
•	1/2 teaspoon ground ginger
•	1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon
•	1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg
•	1/4 teaspoon ground cloves (optional)
•	3 egg yolks

Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat together together:

• 1 1/2 cups (350 g) all-purpose flour
• 1/4 teaspoon salt
• 1 cup (200 g) unsalted butter, chilled and cubed

Use a pastry cutter or two knives to work butter into flour mixture until mixture resembles coarse meal, without overworking or shaping.  This should take about three to five minutes. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least an hour (more preferred).

Of all the philosophers who have influenced Western thought, John Locke is perhaps the most widely studied.  In order to understand what Locke meant by "philosophy", it might be helpful to start by thinking about what "philosophy" means in the widest sense.  Some philosophical ideas are just that — thoughts about things that happen to us or that could happen to us, or about things that already exist, or about things that could possibly exist, or about our place in the world.  At other times, philosophical ideas refer to ideas about some abstract object or property of an object, its logical structure, how to act in certain circumstances, or even the purpose of existence.  For the purposes of this example, we will focus on ideas about existence and continuity in time.  

Locke's view of ethics, for instance, is that our actions are determined by what we believe is right or wrong in every situation, no matter what we know, see, feel, or remember.   To do so, he developed a theory of human nature, which involves two main elements.

First is "reprobation", the capacity we have to judge evil and wrong in our lives and to condemn others who commit evil.  Locke considers it the capacity of human beings to act against their own best interests and benefit from their ignorance, which seems reasonable enough in order to excuse even evil.  Locke regards "reprobation" as our most basic inclination, or as the capacity for negative emotions and bad consequences that we all have.  It is also a concept Locke uses often in his theory of human nature.  

Locke also developed a theory about human beings' place in the world, or about the nature of human beings.  Locke defines "human nature" as having three elements: free will, appetites of self-preservation, and the capacity for pleasure.  Locke regards the capacity for pleasure as being the central aspect in determining most humans' behavior, and also the thing that leads to bad consequences, which he regarded as our most compelling natural motivation or instinct.  

Locke's understanding of human nature is central to his philosophy of ethics, but is not what we will be most concerned with here.  Let's focus instead on Locke's philosophy of politics.  

Locke believes that there are inherent problems with the social order we currently have, and that it will inevitably lead to oppression and suffering.  To prevent this he thinks we need to create a new social order.  Locke thinks that to do so we need to focus on creating a social contract, where each person in a society agrees to certain rules of behavior at certain points in time, which the state then enforces through coercive force.  This idea has become known as the "principle of consent in government".  

There are two major flaws that Locke saw in the current social order.  The first is that people "ought not to" do things that harm others, yet they do.  For instance, people do acts of cruelty to one another on a daily basis.  As Locke developed and articulated this idea of "ought not to", some of his most well-known ideas became "the social contract" which Locke believed must govern our society.  The second flaw Locke saw in the current social order is that people often break their "ought not to" agreements easily and often with little negative consequence.

In order to help us understand Locke's political philosophy, we will use some example texts from his early writings.  These texts can be found in the Dover edition of his works, which also contains most of his later writings.  Let's work through these texts together.  
 
The following passage from An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals by John Locke is an example of political philosophy based on a social contract.   In his first contribution to philosophy, and in the early part of his moral philosophy, Locke focuses on understanding human nature and the limits of our reasoning.  

Men have an inborn tendency to act against their own self-advantage and therefore to have a strong temptation towards evil, though it is not impossible for them at any proper time to be so far removed from it, and from themselves, as not even to see that they suffer from it.

  It is a matter which, now it is said, most nearly defines the character of mankind; and it is the same character that is called into play when either self-restraint or appetite are the leading or governing principles in our conduct.

  Now this inclination towards evil cannot be properly called, as is sometimes supposed, a natural tendency towards corruption and evil; for although it follows that all men ought to use moderation, yet it must sometimes be said that it comes from a power rather than an inclination of the will, especially if we consider also human frailty, which may sometimes restrain one from evil.

  There is no doubt whatever that human nature, as a disposition to evil in some measure, may be conceived in nature alone. 
  For if nature contains sufficient means, even to furnish us with an inclination to evil, it may be well to consider whether it is reasonable or natural for man to try to avoid evil. 
  If it is necessary that we should have an inclination to good and avoid evil, it would appear at any rate that in some degree man's nature ought to try to guide him, and in this connection he has, as usual, to take the guidance of law.  Man, however, does not always choose well, and is not always conscious that he does well; for if this were done often, his action would never seem to be evil. 

  We may therefore think that we have an equal right to assert that a man owes to his society an obligation to be sensible of his duties, and if necessary to avoid them, unless it be necessary to act directly for the public good.

We have, perhaps, had an advantage in this respect over what we otherwise would have been, but it is uncertain whether we have been really helped in so far as we could ever judge, or whether it has only been that society has helped to set up habits that serve our interest. 
  But if we had had no such advantages and were the only individuals that could otherwise have been expected to act for the public good and that we were the only individuals with self-restraint and not corrupted by appetite, we should have found it necessary to act on such a principle from the very first.

  It may again be said, this has nothing to do with reason, unless it is stated that reason should be understood in the sense that it was once thought to be, viz. one that can make us conscious and determine what is right or wrong, unless again the question arises whether we are really conscious as yet of our duty to others. If it’s only dripping a few times a week, and it wouldn’t really be a big deal to fix the leak, go ahead and fix it ASAP. Once you’ve verified that water has entered your house from multiple areas in different ways, you can call your local plumber and have them run their own checks on the pipes. This may involve running a snake to clear your pipes of blockages and inspecting your pipes for cracks. These are things all plumbers will want to do anyway, to make sure they don’t miss any potential problems that could be causing leaks. As the name suggests, a snake is made of rubber, and can be inserted into your pipes below ground level, to check for clogged pipes and prevent blockages from forming. If you only experience slow leaky faucets, and there doesn’t seem to be any flooding or water coming from outside your house, your only option might be to buy some plumbing caulk. prompt: Human: Whats is the best format for a cover letter?
response:
The format of a cover letter varies depending on the job you are applying for, so its best to review the job description and have a general idea of how the company expects the cover letter to be composed.  That being said, here are some common formats:

The traditional way involves starting with your address, phone number, and signature at the top of the page.  Then you list your name, title or position you are applying for, your address and phone number, and your email address.  Then you move on to an introduction to briefly discuss what you know about the company and how your skills align with their needs and goals.  
The introduction could be the first paragraph.

A variant, popular among employers, uses just the company name and logo, followed by an appropriate title, like CEO, and a line which identifies that you are the applicant:  “I am writing to apply for the Director of Sales position that you referred to me about in the January issue of Sales & Marketing.”

In the next paragraph you state what you know about the company.  This paragraph includes a statement about why you are interested in the position, how your skills match the requirements, and how your skills and experience will contribute to the company’s success.

Paragraph three begins with a brief statement about who you are.

The fourth paragraph, followed by your contact information and signature, finishes the letter.

A variant of this format is found in many human resources (HR) job postings where the employer first describes and highlights their strategic goals, then lists the key responsibilities of the position, followed by the requirements.  This format implies the candidate is not the only person applying for the position.  However, in that case, it is the applicant’s responsibility to also describe how their skills match those of the position in the fourth paragraph.

prompt: Human: Is frozen yogurt actually yogurt, or is it just another type of ice cream?
response:
It’s sort of both.  Frozen yogurt is a type of thickened milk beverage that's similar in texture to ice cream, but made by adding gelatin to milk.  The result is called "gelatin ice cream", which has a lower fat content than ice cream.  It includes much more fruit than ice cream.  
There's also "light ice cream", which has less than 1％ fat, but you want to pay attention to the amount of sugar because it tends to be really sweet.

For non-sugar components, there's fruit juice, cream and/or milk solids.  Without gelatin, frozen yogurt is actually a true ice cream, it just has different nutrient proportions.

The ingredients you see on the frozen yogurt container are actually some of the various things that are added to give the frozen yogurt its texture and flavor.  
Some ingredients to look out for include stabilizer (dimethyl glucosamine, guar gum, pectin, xanthan gum), food coloring, and artificial flavor.  
So does that mean frozen yogurt doesn’t actually count as healthy?  It has a lot of fat, sugar, and calories, but it’s still a good alternative to ice cream if you’re trying to reduce the total calories of your day and want some frozen treat.  
It may not be as nutritious as something full of fresh fruit, but then frozen yogurt also has fewer fresh fruits in it than most ice creams.  For something as high in sugar as frozen yogurt it’s a little too high to have as a main meal, but it makes a wonderful snack.  
This article reviews the nutrition facts of some frozen yogurts.  
One interesting aspect is the way other food additives like maltodextrin (corn starch, malt sugar, glucose) can get mixed into frozen yogurt to give it its texture and sweetness, rather than adding any of these directly to the drink. This has led to questions as to whether or not these extra ingredients are healthy.

prompt: Human: Can you tell me how to make chocolate chip cookies?
response:
Of course, I can help you with that.  First you’ll want to measure out 2 1/4 cups of all-purpose flour, 1 tsp of baking soda, and 1 tsp of salt into a bowl.
  
Next, measure out 1 cup of unsalted butter that’s“At least”twice the length of your hand, and put it in a separate bowl. 
  
Then beat the butter with an electric mixer until lighter in color and fluffy, about 3-4 minutes, then gradually mix in an additional 1 tsp of vanilla. 
  
On a different bowl, mix together 2 cups of granulated sugar, 1 large egg, and an additional 1 tsp of vanilla. 
  
Then, while the mixer is on low, slowly fold the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients. 
  
At this point, you’ll need to do some timing, so once your mixer is running smoothly again, slowly pour in 2 1/2 cups of brown sugar, folding briefly after each sip. 
  
After that, measure out 1 cup of chocolate chips, and add them to the dough. 
  
You should now have 2 large, flat bowls, and a 12oz can of semi-sweet chocolate chips mixed inside of the cans. 
  
Pour the brown sugar/chocolate chip mixture containing chocolate chips into one of your bowls, then using a spatula, scrape the chocolate chips out of the other bowl and into the bowl containing the brown sugar/chocolate chip mixture. 
  
Turn the mixer back on to medium speed, add in 3/4 cup of cold water and mix for about 30 seconds, then lower the speed to low and continue mixing until the dough begins to pull away from the side of the bowl, about 60 seconds total. 
  
The final step is to mix a couple more seconds more if the dough still looks crumbly, then scoop the dough into paper-crown shaped balls, place into an ungreased baking sheet (this will make about 3/4th of a batch, depending on how big you want your cookies to be), then flatten each ball slightly with the back of your hand. 
  
The cookies will set as they bake, though you can finish drying them off with a towel if you’d like afterward. 
  
Enjoy your chocolate chip cookies!
